title: Simple Random Walk and Gambler’s Ruin
breadcrumb: Stochastic processes → Random walks → Gambler’s ruin
engineName: Model movement as a random walk, then use boundary conditions and first-step equations to find ruin probabilities and expected duration.
objectives: Define a simple random walk and identify its drift from step probabilities.
Calculate the position distribution after n steps using the number of upward steps.
Set up and solve gambler’s ruin probabilities using first-step recurrence and boundary conditions.
Find expected duration until absorption in the fair and biased cases.
Interpret the fair-game and biased-game results and recognise common boundary and indexing errors.

prereq.name: Binomial distribution
prereq.why: After n independent steps, the number of upward moves is binomial.

prereq.name: Difference equations
prereq.why: Ruin probabilities satisfy a second-order recurrence.

prereq.name: Boundary conditions
prereq.why: Absorbing barriers determine the constants in the recurrence.

traps: Define the state as the current fortune before writing the recurrence.
At an interior state i, p_i = p p_{i+1}+q p_{i−1}; do not reverse p and q.
Use boundary values u_0=0 and u_N=1 when asking for the probability of reaching N before 0.
For a fair walk, the ruin probability from i is 1−i/N; the probability of reaching N first is i/N.
For a biased walk, the ratio q/p determines the powers in the solution.
The expected absorption time for a fair walk is i(N−i), in step units.
Do not confuse eventual ruin probability with expected time to ruin or absorption.
howto: Draw the integer states and absorbing barriers. Define the event being asked, write the first-step recurrence at an interior state, apply both boundary values, and check the answer at the endpoints and at p=q=1/2.

provenance: Original teaching material aligned to the Simple random walk and Gambler’s ruin items in UGC NET Statistics Unit IX. Practice questions are original and are not represented as official UGC NET PYQs.

sheet: A simple random walk moves +1 with probability p and −1 with probability q=1−p.
After n steps, S_n=S_0+2X−n where X~Binomial(n,p).
The drift per step is E[ΔS]=p−q=2p−1.
In gambler’s ruin, fortune i moves to i+1 with probability p and i−1 with probability q.
With barriers 0 and N, both endpoints are absorbing.
Let u_i=P_i(reach N before 0): u_0=0, u_N=1 and u_i=pu_{i+1}+qu_{i−1}.
If p=q=1/2, u_i=i/N and ruin probability is 1−i/N.
For a fair walk, expected absorption time is i(N−i).
For p≠q, expected absorption time is [i−Nu_i]/(q−p).
cards: Up with p; down with q=1−p.
1−u_i when u_i is probability of hitting N before 0.
u_0=0 and u_N=1 for reaching N before 0.
tricks: Check which boundary is the success event before writing u_0 and u_N.
If p=q, use the linear solution; do not substitute q/p=1 into a 0/0 expression.
For p≠q, verify u_0=0 and u_N=1 after substitution.
At p=1/2, expected duration is largest near the midpoint and zero at either boundary.
shortcuts: Fair walk: success probability i/N; ruin probability (N−i)/N.
One-step drift is positive, zero or negative according as p is greater than, equal to or less than 1/2.
At i=N/2 in a fair walk, expected absorption time is N²/4.
remember: Probability of reaching the upper barrier and probability of ruin are complementary when absorption occurs at one of the two barriers.
First-step equations condition on the first move, not on the final path.

scenes.title: Refresh steps, binomial counts and recurrences
scenes.objective: Rebuild the tools used in random-walk calculations.
body: A simple random walk changes its position by one unit at each step. An upward step is +1 and a downward step is −1.
If each step is upward with probability p and downward with probability q=1−p, then the number X of upward steps in n independent moves has a Binomial(n,p) distribution.
After n steps, the net change is X−(n−X)=2X−n. This converts a path question into a binomial probability calculation.

items.ask: If there are n steps and X upward moves, how many downward moves occur?
refresh: Every step is either upward or downward.
The total number of steps is the sum of the two counts.

items.ask: What is the net displacement after n steps?
What is the expected change in one step?
refresh: The step is +1 with probability p and −1 with probability q.

ask.q: Which distribution counts upward steps in n independent moves?
ask.nudge: Each step is a Bernoulli trial.

scenes.title: A fortune that moves one unit at a time
scenes.objective: Interpret a random walk and absorbing barriers.
body: Imagine a player whose fortune changes by one unit after every game. A win adds one unit; a loss removes one unit.
The player stops when the fortune reaches zero or a fixed target N. These two endpoints are absorbing: after reaching either endpoint, the game ends.
The central question is often whether the player reaches the target before going broke. This is gambler’s ruin, a random walk with two absorbing barriers.

scenario.teaser: A player starts with a limited stake
scenario.title: A game between two fortunes
body: A player begins with 3 units. A win increases the fortune by one, and a loss decreases it by one. The game ends if the player reaches 0 or 7 units.

The state is the current fortune, so the possible transient states are 1,2,3,4,5,6. State 0 is ruin and state 7 is the target. At each interior state, the next state is one step higher with probability p and one step lower with probability q=1−p.
We want the probability of reaching 7 before 0. The first move determines whether the next problem is the same problem starting from 4 or from 2. This observation produces a recurrence.
scenario.q: What are the two absorbing states in this game?

ask.q: Why are states 0 and N called absorbing barriers?
ask.nudge: The game stops when either is reached.

scenes.title: Simple random walk and its distribution
scenes.objective: Calculate the position after n independent steps.

blocks.body: S_n=S_0+X_1+⋯+X_n, where each increment is +1 with probability p and −1 with probability q=1−p, independently.
If X is the number of upward steps, X~Binomial(n,p) and S_n=S_0+2X−n.

ask.q: Starting at 0, what is the probability of being at position 2 after 4 steps?
ask.nudge: Solve 2X−4=2 for the required number of upward steps.

scenes.title: Worked example: a position after four steps
scenes.objective: Use a binomial count to find a random-walk probability.
scenes.problem: A walk starts at 0. Each step is +1 with probability 1/2 and −1 with probability 1/2. Find P(S₄=2).

steps.say: Translate the final position into upward steps.
steps.why: Three upward moves and one downward move produce net position 2.
The four steps are independent and have the same upward probability.
Exactly three of the four moves must be upward.
There are four equally likely sequences with three upward moves.

ask.q: Can the walk be at position 2 after three steps if it starts at zero?
ask.nudge: The parity of position changes with each step.

scenes.objective: Set up the first-step recurrence and boundary conditions.

blocks.body: Let u_i=P_i(the walk reaches N before 0), starting at fortune i.

flow.title: Gambler’s ruin solution plan

ask.q: If the player starts at N, what is u_N?
ask.nudge: The target has already been reached.

scenes.title: Worked example: fair gambler’s ruin
scenes.problem: A fair player starts with 2 units and stops at 0 or 5. Find the probability of reaching 5 before 0.

steps.why: The event is reaching 5 before ruin at 0.

steps.say: The solution is linear in i.

steps.why: The boundary conditions determine the constants.
The chance of reaching 5 first is 2/5; ruin probability is 3/5.

ask.q: What is the probability of ruin before reaching 5?

scenes.title: Biased gambler’s ruin
scenes.objective: Use the geometric solution when p and q differ.

blocks.body: When p=q=1/2, the recurrence has the linear solution u_i=i/N; do not substitute q/p=1 into the biased formula without taking a limit.
If p>q, upward movement is favoured; if p<q, downward movement is favoured. The same boundary event and formula still apply.

ask.q: In the biased formula, what is q/p when the game is fair?

scenes.title: Guided problem: a biased game
scenes.objective: Calculate an upper-barrier probability using the biased formula.
scenes.problem: A player starts at 1 unit, with barriers 0 and 3. The chance of a win is p=2/3 and q=1/3. Find the probability of reaching 3 before 0.
hints: First identify that the desired event is reaching the upper barrier, so u₀=0 and u₃=1.
Substitute i=1 and N=3 into the biased formula.

scenario.teaser: A player has a favourable game
scenario.title: A three-unit target
body: A player begins with one unit and must reach three units before losing everything. Each play is a win with probability 2/3 and a loss with probability 1/3.
The upper-barrier probability is found from the biased gambler’s ruin formula. The ratio q/p is 1/2, and the boundaries are 0 and 3.
The calculation gives 4/7 for reaching the target first. The complementary probability 3/7 is the probability of ruin first.
scenario.q: Is the probability of reaching the target greater than one-half?
scenario.answer: Yes. It is 4/7, reflecting the favourable upward step probability.

ask.q: Why is q/p rather than p/q used in this expression?
ask.nudge: Check that the formula satisfies u₀=0 and u_N=1.

scenes.title: Expected time until absorption
scenes.objective: Distinguish expected duration from ruin probability.

blocks.body: Let m_i be the expected number of steps to hit either 0 or N, starting from i.
For p≠q, m_i=[i−N u_i]/(q−p), where u_i is the probability of reaching N before 0.

ask.q: What is the expected absorption time for a fair walk starting at i=2 with N=5?

scenes.title: Worked example: expected duration in a fair game
scenes.objective: Calculate the expected number of steps to absorption.
scenes.problem: A fair walk starts at fortune 2 and is absorbed at 0 or 5. Find the expected number of steps until absorption.

steps.why: For p=q=1/2, this solves the expected-time recurrence with zero boundary values.

steps.say: Substitute the starting fortune and upper barrier.
steps.why: The walk begins at i=2 and N=5.
The expected duration is six steps.

ask.q: At which starting fortune is the fair expected duration largest when N=6?
ask.nudge: The product i(6−i) is largest nearest the midpoint.

scenes.title: Trap check: boundaries, bias and duration
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false, then read the reason.

items.claim: For u_i=P_i(reach N before 0), the boundary values are u₀=0 and u_N=1.
items.why: At zero the success event is impossible; at N it has already occurred.

items.claim: For a fair walk, the probability of reaching N before 0 is (N−i)/N.
items.why: That is the ruin probability. The upper-barrier probability is i/N.

items.claim: The first-step equation at an interior state is u_i=p u_{i+1}+q u_{i−1}.
items.why: Condition on the first upward or downward step.

items.claim: The expected absorption time of a fair walk is i(N−i).
items.why: This is the solution of the fair expected-time recurrence with zero boundary values.

items.claim: The probability of ruin and the probability of reaching N first add to one.
items.why: The walk is absorbed at one of the two barriers.

ask.q: Which boundary condition changes if the event of interest is ruin before reaching N?
ask.nudge: Redefine the success event before assigning boundary values.
